abstract: Detecting multiple viruses in biofluids such as saliva remains challenging because viral proteins are of low abundance, embedded in a complex matrix, and subject to rapid sequence variation. Mass spectrometry-based proteomics complements nucleic acid-based assays by directly resolving protein-level sequence variation, but standard database cross-correlation searches lose sensitivity as viral variant sequences increase the database size. Here, we report a sequence-filtering strategy integrated with single amino acid variant (SAAV) detection to enable sensitive mutation variant detection while minimizing the loss of search sensitivity. In silico analysis of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza sequences reveals bimodal prevalence distributions of the mutated peptides. By using a three-month time window and removing low-prevalence peptides, the peptide database size is reduced by 82.1% for SARS-CoV-2 and 94.6% for influenza at a 10% prevalence threshold with only a <0.8% loss in search sensitivity while retaining 97.8% and 98.4% of viral peptides in the subsequent month. A mutation discovery module further mitigates loss of database coverage and improves variant detection in peptide-spiked saliva experiments compared with de novo sequencing, achieving SAAV peptide-spectrum match recovery rates of 73.6% for the SARS-CoV-2 spike and 88.4% for H1N1 hemagglutinin. This study establishes a scalable proteomics framework for the sensitive detection of known and emerging viral variants in complex biofluid matrices.
